Interpretability research · open-source models · run on a laptop



I’m an engineer on a path from full-stack and cloud to AI, now focused on model interpretability. Here I take concrete problem statements about model behaviour and test them directly inside open models, publishing all the code, so that AI becomes something we can look inside and make safer.

title: Opening up language models to see how they actually work
text:
Why interpretability
Every system I’ve worked on had a way to look inside it. With traditional software you read the code. With cloud systems you have logs, metrics and traces. With large language models, we ship systems we can’t inspect: we see the input and the output, and the reasoning in between is a black box.
That gap worries me. As models take on more consequential work, “it seemed to work in testing” isn’t enough. Interpretability is the closest thing we have to observability for AI: tools to see what a model represents, where a behaviour comes from, and whether we can correct it.

title: Opening up language models to see how they actually work
text:
What I research


Where knowledge lives
Tracing at which layer a model “knows” a fact, and what it was considering before.


Why models behave as they do
Finding the internal features and circuits behind refusals, sycophancy and mistakes.


Steering and control
Testing whether changing what’s inside a model changes what it does.

title: About
text:
This blog documents independent research on AI model visibility: understanding what language models represent internally and why they behave the way they do.
Every post starts from a concrete problem statement, tests it with interpretability tools (TransformerLens, SAELens, nnsight, Gemma Scope) on open-source models, and ships the full code so anyone can reproduce it.
All experiments run locally on a MacBook (Apple Silicon, 48 GB).
